title: Global Consumers Have Moved On. Has Your Growth Strategy Caught Up?
gist: BCG's 13,000-consumer, 12-market survey finds five durable shifts reshaping demand: value beats price, longevity-seeking is displacing wealth as the marker of success, solo households are a large underserved high-spend segment, trust is consolidating around experts/peers/AI rather than brands, and AI is already deciding roughly a third of purchase journeys while adoption runs furthest ahead in developing markets.

insights.claim: 67% of consumers say they will not buy a product they can afford if it doesn't deliver perceived value, meaning price only earns a product a spot in the consideration set while a separate value judgment decides the actual purchase.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Brands competing purely on price discounting are optimizing the wrong lever; value drivers like quality, convenience, and trust predict purchase far better than affordability.
insights.quote: In our survey, 67% of consumers said they would not buy a product, even when they could afford it, if they did not perceive strong value.
insights.locator: Value Is the Currency—Price Is Just the Entry Ticket

insights.claim: Despite years of consumer signaling that value matters more than price, only 14% of the 1,000+ brands BCG analyzed consistently win on value, revealing a large execution gap between recognized consumer priorities and actual brand delivery.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: This gap is a strategic opening: a company that systematically closes it on quality, convenience, and trust can win share from competitors still fighting on price.
insights.quote: only 14% of the 1,000+ brands we analyzed consistently win on value
insights.locator: Value Is the Currency—Price Is Just the Entry Ticket

insights.claim: In automotive, service and convenience are key value drivers, yet only 5% of auto brands stand out for service quality; in packaged snacks, where quantity is a critical value component, only 6% of brands are seen as delivering the right amount for consumers' needs.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Category-specific value gaps in service (auto) and portion sizing (snacks) are quantifiable, underexploited openings for share gain.
insights.quote: only 5% of brands stand out for their service quality
insights.locator: Many organizations have yet to deliver on the dimensions of value

insights.claim: Quality has become the single most important driver of value satisfaction across categories and now functions as a baseline expectation rather than a differentiator, with price/promotions, personal connection, volume, service, and convenience layered on as category-specific value drivers.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Treat quality as table stakes and compete on whichever secondary value dimension is most salient for the specific category and occasion.
insights.quote: Quality is the single most important driver of value satisfaction, and it has become a baseline expectation.
insights.locator: Quality is the single most important driver of value satisfaction

insights.claim: Nearly three-quarters of consumers now rank health and well-being as the top marker of a prosperous life, well ahead of career (40%) and financial wealth (28%), indicating that the definition of 'success' is shifting away from money and status.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Consumer and even financial-services brands should test health/longevity-based positioning against traditional wealth-status messaging, which may be losing resonance.
insights.quote: Nearly three-quarters of consumers in our survey ranked health and well-being as the strongest indicator of prosperity, ahead of career (40%) and financial wealth (28%).
insights.locator: Longevity and Well-Being Are Core Life Ambitions

insights.claim: A 'longevity seeker' segment that prioritizes healthy aging already represents nearly 40% of consumers, grew 4 percentage points in the past year alone, and skews toward affluent Gen X and Baby Boomer households in OECD economies.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: This fast-growing, high-spending cohort cuts across nutrition, fitness, beauty, preventive healthcare, and financial planning, warranting a coordinated cross-category growth strategy rather than siloed category plans.
insights.quote: This cohort already represents nearly four in ten consumers today, and it has grown by 4 percentage points over the past year.
insights.locator: we identified a group that we refer to as longevity seekers

insights.claim: Longevity-minded consumers are defined more by avoidance than adoption: they reject unhealthy habits like fast food, binge eating, alcohol, and tobacco roughly twice as forcefully as they embrace good habits, a behavioral asymmetry many incumbent food, beverage, and tobacco brands failed to anticipate.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Categories exposed to indulgence products should model downside volume risk from longevity-driven avoidance, not just upside from wellness-product adoption.
insights.quote: They reject unhealthy habits such as fast food, binge eating, and alcohol and tobacco use twice as forcefully as they adopt good habits.
insights.locator: Their defining behavior is avoidance

insights.claim: GLP-1 drug adoption in the US has grown more than eightfold since 2020 to roughly 16 million users and is projected to double again by 2030, while European adoption has reached about 9 million users with an expected total above 20 million by 2030 — and this pharmaceutical shift is already reshaping demand in food, beverage, apparel, beauty, and fitness well beyond healthcare.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: GLP-1 penetration is a trackable leading indicator for volume and mix shifts in packaged food, snacking, apparel sizing, and fitness spend, worth building into category demand models now.
insights.quote: the number of GLP-1 users has grown more than eightfold since 2020 to an estimated 16 million people and is projected to double again by 2030
insights.locator: The rapid adoption of GLP-1 therapies

insights.claim: 30% of households in mature markets are now single-person households, up 6 percentage points since 2010, reaching roughly 40% in Germany, Sweden, France, and Italy and approaching similar levels in Japan and South Korea.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Solo living is a structural, near-majority household type in several major developed economies, so product and channel strategy built around family units is increasingly mismatched with reality.
insights.quote: Today, 30% of households in mature markets consist of a single person
insights.locator: Living Alone Is a Choice—and a Statement

insights.claim: Solo households spend two to three times more per capita than multiperson households, yet 50%-70% of solo consumers say products and services aren't designed for them, making single-person households simultaneously one of the highest-value and most underserved consumer segments.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Brands that redesign pack sizes, delivery thresholds, and promotions away from bulk-discount logic can capture share from a high-spending, currently poorly-served segment.
insights.quote: Solo households spend two to three times more per capita than multiperson households do, yet 50% to 70% of solo householders in our survey told us that products and services are not designed for people like them.
insights.locator: Solo households spend two to three times more per capita

insights.claim: Solo consumers' purchase journeys have roughly 30% fewer touchpoints than multiperson households', correlating with stronger brand loyalty, yet solo households also shop offline more often — not by preference but because delivery minimums, at-home delivery/return requirements, and bulk packaging are structured for family households.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: E-commerce and logistics operators should redesign delivery thresholds and package formats specifically for single-person orders to capture currently-leaking offline demand.
insights.quote: with roughly 30% fewer touchpoints, and this contributes to stronger brand loyalty
insights.locator: The purchase journeys of solo consumers are more compressed

insights.claim: Solo households could exceed 45% of all households in Japan and Germany by 2050, which BCG says will force a rethink of categories built around shared-household assumptions (life and health insurance, pension products, home ownership, automotive) while creating growth room in food/beverage, restaurants, hospitality, pet care, and household services designed for independent living.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Insurers, pension providers, and homebuilders with product designs anchored to multi-person households face a structural headwind that will show up first in Japan and Germany.
insights.quote: potentially exceeding 45% of households in Japan and Germany by 2050
insights.locator: The solo household is emerging as one of the largest

insights.claim: 43% of consumers feel mentally overwhelmed by information volume and more than half say they don't fully trust any single source, so consumers are concentrating trust in a narrow set of sources — experts, friends/family, and increasingly AI tools — none of which brands directly control.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Since brands can't buy their way into these trusted channels, marketing budget should shift toward earning third-party validation (expert endorsement, word of mouth, AI-legible product data) rather than paid reach.
insights.quote: brands do not control any of these trusted sources
insights.locator: Consumers Are Building a New Trust Compass with AI

insights.claim: AI is the fastest-growing source of trusted information: 30% of consumers say they completely trust AI tools today, and another 15% expect to trust them by 2030, putting AI on track to be trusted by nearly half of consumers within a few years.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Trust in AI as a recommendation source is compounding quickly; brands need AI-legible, verifiable product data now, before this trust curve matures and locks in default recommenders.
insights.quote: 30% of survey respondents completely trust them now, and an additional 15% expect to do so by 2030
insights.locator: AI tools are also gaining trust faster than other sources

insights.claim: Even as trust in AI grows, 60% of consumers still limit how much personal or sensitive information they share with AI tools, showing AI trust today is conditional and could stall without rigorous transparency and responsible-use practices.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Don't extrapolate AI-trust growth linearly; a privacy or misuse incident could sharply reverse adoption, so companies embedding AI in commerce should over-invest in transparency safeguards.
insights.quote: 60% of consumers still limit the amount of personal or sensitive information they share with AI tools
insights.locator: Although AI's influence continues to grow rapidly

insights.claim: 31% of surveyed consumers already use AI at least occasionally in purchase journeys, 19% are 'AI loyalists' who rely on it regularly, and 70% of those loyalists ultimately buy whatever product AI recommends — AI has become a hidden but decisive purchase driver most brands haven't planned for.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: AI recommendation algorithms are becoming as important a distribution channel as shelf placement or search ranking, and most companies have no visibility into how they're ranked there.
insights.quote: 31% of surveyed consumers already use AI at least occasionally in their purchase journeys, 19% are AI loyalists who rely on it regularly, and 70% of these loyalists ultimately buy the products that AI recommends
insights.locator: The Age of AI-Driven Decisions

insights.claim: AI usage in purchase journeys has roughly tripled in 18 months and is most concentrated among the consumers brands most want to reach: 50% of developing-market consumers, 43% of higher-income households, and 42% of Gen Z/Millennials already use AI in purchase decisions.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Emerging-market and younger, affluent consumers are leapfrogging to AI-mediated shopping; brands targeting these segments should prioritize AI-channel optimization over traditional digital marketing.
insights.quote: roughly triple the level reported just 18 months ago
insights.locator: AI Is Becoming a Powerful Voice in Consumer Choice

insights.claim: AI-driven purchasing is far more advanced in developing markets than developed ones: 50% of developing-market consumers use AI in purchase journeys, 36% rely on it regularly, and 26% buy on its recommendations, versus 26%, 14%, and 10% respectively in developed markets — a reversal of the usual pattern of developed markets leading consumer-tech adoption.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Consumer companies should treat developing markets as the leading indicator and testbed for AI-commerce strategy rather than assuming developed markets will show the way first.
insights.quote: 50% of consumers use AI in their purchase journeys, 36% rely on it regularly, and 26% buy on the basis of its recommendations, compared with 26%, 14%, and 10%, respectively, in developed markets
insights.locator: The change is particularly pronounced in developing markets

insights.claim: In roughly 63% of AI-assisted purchase journeys, AI introduces the consumer to a brand they would not otherwise have considered, meaning AI is displacing traditional brand-awareness advertising as the mechanism that builds the consideration set.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: For challenger brands, AI recommendation is now a lower-cost path to consideration than paid advertising; for incumbents, auditing AI visibility is a new core competitive-intelligence task.
insights.quote: AI introduces consumers to brands that they would not otherwise have considered in roughly 63% of AI-assisted purchase journeys
insights.locator: AI assembles that shortlist on the consumer's behalf

insights.claim: One leading AI platform grew from 350 million to 900 million monthly active users in just 13 months, illustrating the speed at which AI adoption — and by extension AI's influence over consumer purchase decisions — is compounding.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Leading AI platforms' user-growth curves are now a leading indicator worth tracking for consumer-facing companies, akin to smartphone or social-platform adoption curves in prior cycles.
insights.quote: one leading platform growing from 350 million to 900 million monthly active users in just 13 months
insights.locator: AI usage more than doubled in the past year

insights.claim: Shopping is likely to evolve in stages from today's AI-assisted discovery to AI-enabled transactions and eventually to autonomous AI purchasing agents that transact on consumers' behalf, meaning the brands that ultimately win will be those AI itself determines are most relevant.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: This implies a long-term shift of brand competition from consumer-facing marketing to algorithm-facing optimization, a discipline analogous to SEO but for AI purchasing agents.
insights.quote: shopping is likely to evolve from AI-assisted discovery to AI-enabled transactions and, in some cases, to autonomous purchasing agents that act on consumers
insights.locator: Today's AI-assisted recommendations represent only the first stage

insights.claim: Attention spans have fallen 69% since 2004 and ad-blocking usage has increased 21-fold, while 43% of consumers report feeling mentally overwhelmed — a structural erosion of the attention-based advertising model that predates and compounds the shift toward AI-mediated discovery.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Paid-attention advertising economics are deteriorating structurally, reinforcing the case for shifting budget toward trust-building and AI-channel presence rather than reach-based ad spend.
insights.quote: Attention spans have fallen by 69% since 2004, ad blocking has increased 21-fold, and 43% of consumers report feeling mentally overwhelmed.
insights.locator: A World of Always-On Digital Life

insights.claim: Global life expectancy has risen six to eight years since 2000, pushing back traditional life milestones and extending the period of independent living — a demographic tailwind BCG links directly to both the longevity-seeker segment and the rise of solo households.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Longevity and solo-living themes are downstream effects of a multi-decade demographic shift, so related spending categories have a durable multi-decade tailwind, not a fad.
insights.quote: Globally, life expectancy has increased by six to eight years since 2000
insights.locator: A World of Longer, Wealthier Lives

insights.claim: Among Baby Boomers, 55% cite geopolitical conflict and 45% cite economic uncertainty as major sources of feeling mentally overwhelmed, versus 42% and 41% respectively for Gen Z, showing older, wealthier cohorts report more macro anxiety than younger consumers.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Safety- and stability-oriented messaging may resonate more with Boomer spending decisions than assumptions that younger generations are the most anxious cohort.
insights.quote: 55% cite geopolitical conflict and 45% economic uncertainty as major contributors to feelings of being mentally overwhelmed, compared with 42% and 41%, respectively, among members of Gen Z
insights.locator: These concerns are particularly pronounced among Baby Boomers

insights.claim: BCG frames a six-part playbook for consumer companies: compete on value not price; build around tomorrow's growth segments (solo households, longevity seekers, AI natives); earn trust through third-party-verifiable evidence; prepare for AI-native/zero-click commerce; modernize consumer-insight capabilities to track real-time shifts rather than explain past behavior; and build commercial capabilities that evolve as fast as consumers do.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: This is a ready-made diagnostic checklist for evaluating whether a consumer company's strategy, insights function, and commercial model are aligned with where demand is actually moving.
insights.locator: Six Imperatives to Capture the Next Wave of Growth

insights.claim: BCG warns that brands which haven't audited their AI presence risk being excluded from consumer consideration before the purchase journey even begins, and urges companies to encode explicit brand guardrails into their 'agentic marketing stack' so AI represents them accurately.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Auditing how AI assistants describe, rank, and recommend a company's products should become a standing marketing-ops function, akin to how SEO audits became standard once search engines became gatekeepers.
insights.quote: Brands that have not audited their AI presence may find themselves excluded from consideration before a consumer’s purchase journey has even begun.
insights.locator: Prepare for a World of AI-Native Commerce

insights.claim: Traditional demographic segmentation by age, income, and geography is becoming a weaker predictor of consumer demand than behavioral/values-based segments like longevity seekers, solo households, and AI natives, which cut across those traditional categories.
insights.speaker: https://www.bcg.com/about/people/experts/aparna-bharadwaj
insights.so_what: Companies whose portfolios are still organized around classic demographic segments should re-segment around cross-cutting behavioral cohorts to find where growth is actually concentrated.
insights.quote: Traditional demographic segments are becoming weaker predictors of demand.
insights.locator: Build Around Tomorrow's Growth Segments
